question: A
title: Affordable Housing
explanation: The City Council asked voters to approve borrowing up to $22 million for affordable housing, such as buying and fixing up run-down property, building or renovating homes, and helping people rent or buy.
if_for: The city would be able to borrow the money. Which projects get it, and when, would be decided later.
if_against: The city would not be able to borrow this money, so affordable housing work would need other funding.

question: B
title: School Facilities
explanation: The City Council asked voters to approve borrowing up to $60 million for public schools: building and fixing school buildings, buying equipment, and improving athletic facilities, including some that also serve community health and recreation.
if_for: The city would be able to borrow the money for school facilities. Which schools get it would be decided later.
if_against: The city would not be able to borrow this money, so school building work would need other funding.

question: C
title: Community And Economic Development
explanation: The City Council asked voters to approve borrowing up to $50 million for neighborhood and economic development: cleaning up blighted property, improving neighborhoods, helping people with housing, and supporting businesses.
if_for: The city would be able to borrow the money and use it for loans and grants as well as direct projects. Which ones get funded would be decided later.
if_against: The city would not be able to borrow this money, so this kind of development work would need other funding.

question: D
title: Public Infrastructure
explanation: The City Council asked voters to approve borrowing up to $148 million for public infrastructure: city buildings, libraries, parks, streets, utilities, technology, and similar improvements.
if_for: The city would be able to borrow the money. Which projects get it would be decided later.
if_against: The city would not be able to borrow this money, so infrastructure work would need other funding.

question: E
title: Contract Bidding And Awards
explanation: Right now the city charter says contracts must go to the lowest bidder, sets a way to break ties, and requires certain bonds from contractors. The City Council asked voters to take those rules out of the charter.
if_for: Those rules would be removed on November 7, 2028, unless the city passes its own rules on the topic sooner. The city could then change how it awards contracts through city laws or regulations, without going back to voters.
if_against: The current charter rules on bidding would stay in place.

question: F
title: Budget Process And Board Of Estimates
explanation: The City Council asked voters to change how the city passes laws and builds its budget. The mayor, not the Board of Estimates, would prepare the budget, and the Board would lose many of its other duties, which could be handed to other city offices. It would also shorten the time to veto a bill and override a veto, end the preliminary budget hearings, and remove the $1 million limit on the emergency fund.
if_for: The changes would start on different dates: December 3, 2026 for most of them, November 7, 2028 for charter sections that are removed (unless the city replaces them sooner), and December 5, 2028 for the new veto and approval rules.
if_against: Nothing would change: the Board of Estimates would keep its current duties, and the current budget and veto rules would stay.

question: G
title: Franchises And Minor Privileges
explanation: The City Council asked voters to update the rules for how outside parties can use city property. The stormwater system could never be sold or rented out. Space in the city's conduit system could be rented out, but the conduit system itself still couldn't be sold. Minor privileges (small permissions to use part of city property) would be granted by a city agency under a process set by city law, instead of by the Board of Estimates. It would also remove outdated language about street railways and trackless trolleys.
if_for: Most changes would start December 3, 2026. Removed charter sections would go away on November 7, 2028, unless the city replaces them sooner.
if_against: The current charter language would stay, including the Board of Estimates' role in granting minor privileges.

question: H
title: Department Of Water And Wastewater
explanation: The City Council asked voters to create a new city Department of Water and Wastewater with its own director. Responsibility for the water supply and wastewater systems would move over from the Department of Public Works. It would also remove the charter requirement that bureaus within Public Works be created or eliminated by city law.
if_for: The new department would take over on January 1
explanation_source_id: Water and wastewater would stay with the Department of Public Works.

question: I
title: Baltimore Baby Fund
explanation: Residents who signed a petition asked voters to create the Baltimore Baby Fund, a separate pot of city money to help improve the financial stability of families with newborns. The city would have to put money in every year, and the fund could also accept donations and grants.
if_for: The fund would be created. Each year the city would have to add 3 cents for every $100 of taxable property value. The money could only be used for families with newborns, and it couldn't replace newborn funding already in this year's budget.

question: A
title: Affordable Housing Loan
explanation: The City Council asked voters to approve borrowing up to $20 million for affordable housing, such as buying and fixing up property, building or renovating homes, helping people rent or buy, and supporting the Affordable Housing Trust Fund.
if_for: The city would be able to borrow the money. Which projects get it would be decided later.
if_against: The city would not be able to borrow this money through this question. Existing housing programs wouldn't end because of it.

question: B
title: School Loan
explanation: The City Council asked voters to approve borrowing up to $55 million for public schools: buying or improving school property, building and rebuilding schools, buying equipment, and improving athletic and other school facilities.
if_for: The city would be able to borrow the money for school projects. Which schools get it would be decided later.
if_against: The city would not be able to borrow this money through this question. Other school funding wouldn't be affected.

question: C
title: Community And Economic Development Loan
explanation: The City Council asked voters to approve borrowing up to $50 million for neighborhood and economic development: redeveloping property, business and job programs, homeownership and home repair help, cultural projects, and tourism.
if_for: The city would be able to borrow the money and use it for loans and grants as well as direct projects. Which ones get funded would be decided later.
if_against: The city would not be able to borrow this money through this question. Other development programs wouldn't end because of it.

question: D
title: Public Infrastructure
explanation: The City Council asked voters to approve borrowing up to $125 million for public infrastructure: streets, bridges, city buildings, libraries, parks, recreation facilities, technology, and trees.
if_for: The city would be able to borrow the money. Which projects get it would be decided later.
if_against: The city would not be able to borrow this money through this question. Infrastructure work paid for from other sources could still go ahead.

question: E
title: Baltimore City Police Department
explanation: The City Council asked voters to write the Police Department into the city charter as a city agency headed by a Police Commissioner. The mayor would appoint the commissioner, subject to confirmation, and the commissioner would decide how the department is organized and run. The charter would also spell out the department's job (keeping the peace, preventing and investigating crime, enforcing laws, and making arrests) and set the process for creating police districts.
if_for: The department, the commissioner's role and powers, and the officers' duties would become part of the charter.
if_against: These provisions wouldn't be added to the charter.

question: F
title: Inner Harbor Park
explanation: The City Council asked voters to change a charter rule that dedicates the Inner Harbor shoreline to public park use. Up to 4.5 acres (up from 3.2) near Conway Street could be used for restaurants, businesses, multifamily housing, and parking. Areas used for housing and parking would no longer count as part of the public park.
if_for: The land-use changes would be adopted, and the area allowed for these uses would grow from 3.2 to 4.5 acres. Approval alone wouldn't mean anything gets built.
if_against: The current charter restriction would stay in place.

question: G
title: Community Reinvestment And Reparations Fund
explanation: The City Council asked voters to create a city fund to pay for the work of the Community Reinvestment and Reparations Commission. Money in it would carry over from year to year instead of expiring, and it could only be used for the commission's work, within limits set by state law.
if_for: The fund would exist, and the City Council could pass laws on how it is overseen and run. The question doesn't set a dollar amount.

question: H
title: Reducing The Size Of The City Council
explanation: Residents who signed a petition asked voters to shrink the City Council from 14 districts to 8. If it passed, the mayor would have to draw a new district map based on the latest census and give it to the Council by February 1 of the first municipal election year afterward.
if_for: The Council would go down to 8 districts, and the mayor would draw new districts.
if_against: The Council would stay at 14 districts.
